preamble: The rising diphthong /ue/ ([we]) loses its labial-velar onset and reduces to plain /e/. The best-documented case is a sporadic late Old Spanish change, mostly after a consonant + liquid cluster (fruente > frente, flueco > fleco, culuebra > culebra) and in some suffixes (-uelo/-uero beside -elo/-ero); its conditioning, phonetic or morphological, is debated. It parallels the Old Spanish reduction of ie to i (Castiella > Castilla).

examples.note: Wiktionary: frente is inherited from Old Spanish fruente; the [we] from stressed Latin ŏ lost its glide after fr-.
Wiktionary: from older flueco; same reduction of [we] to [e] after fl-.

examples.from: Old Spanish culuebra (< Vulgar Latin *colobra, Latin colubra)
examples.note: Wiktionary: inherited from Old Spanish culuebra; [we] reduced to [e] after bl.

sources: Malkiel, Y. (1976). Multi-Conditioned Sound Change and the Impact of Morphology on Phonology. Language, 52(4), 757-778. https://doi.org/10.2307/413294

Méndez Dosuna, J., & Pensado, C. (1986). Can Phonological Changes Really Have a Morphological Origin? The Case of Old Spanish ie > i and ue > e. Diachronica, 3(2), 185-201. https://doi.org/10.1075/dia.3.2.04men
